deep-rest.name: Deep Rest
deep-rest.tagline: A slow delta bed for winding all the way down.
deep-rest.description: A steady 2.5 Hz delta beat over warm brown noise. Lie back, let the room go quiet, and let the hour carry you. May support deeper relaxation before sleep.

midnight-tide.name: Midnight Tide
midnight-tide.tagline: Long, low swells for the middle of the night.
midnight-tide.description: A very slow 1.5 Hz pulse that rolls like distant surf under deep brown noise. Built for long listening once the lights are out.

slow-wave-drift.name: Slow Wave Drift
slow-wave-drift.tagline: One beat per second. Nothing else to do.
slow-wave-drift.description: A 1 Hz delta beat, about the pace of a resting heart, layered with soft pink noise to mask household sounds.

lullaby-174.name: Lullaby 174
lullaby-174.tagline: The lowest solfeggio tone under a gentle delta beat.
lullaby-174.description: A 2 Hz delta beat paired with a quiet 174 Hz solfeggio tone and brown noise. Simple, round, and very low.

cloud-harbor.name: Cloud Harbor
cloud-harbor.tagline: A soft landing at the end of a long day.
cloud-harbor.description: Thirty minutes of 3 Hz delta over airy pink noise. A good first session if you are new to sleep frequencies.

night-garden.name: Night Garden
night-garden.tagline: Warm, dark and slow, like a garden after rain.
night-garden.description: A 3.5 Hz beat sitting on the edge of delta and theta, with deep brown noise underneath.

dream-gate.name: Dream Gate
dream-gate.tagline: Theta for the drifting moments before sleep.
dream-gate.description: A 4.5 Hz theta beat for the hazy, image-filled stretch between waking and sleep.

full-sleep-cycle.name: Full Sleep Cycle
full-sleep-cycle.tagline: Two hours of the slowest beat in the catalog.
full-sleep-cycle.description: A 0.8 Hz delta beat at a low 110 Hz carrier under brown noise. Set the timer and let it fade out on its own.

velvet-dark.name: Velvet Dark
velvet-dark.description: A 2 Hz delta beat wrapped in thick brown noise. Designed to sound like nothing at all after a few minutes.

moon-breath.name: Moon Breath
moon-breath.tagline: Breathe with the pulse and let your thoughts thin out.
moon-breath.description: A short 3 Hz session with soft pink noise. Try slowing your breath until each exhale lasts about five beats.

late-night-unwind.name: Late Night Unwind
late-night-unwind.tagline: For when your mind is still running at bedtime.
late-night-unwind.description: A 5.5 Hz theta beat to help shift gears after screens and conversation. May support relaxation before sleep.

power-nap.name: Power Nap
power-nap.tagline: Twenty minutes, then back to your day.
power-nap.description: A short delta session sized for a nap. The fade-out at the end is deliberately gentle.

theta-temple.name: Theta Temple
theta-temple.tagline: A spacious 6 Hz theta field for sitting practice.
theta-temple.description: A classic 6 Hz theta beat over light pink noise. Sit comfortably, follow the breath, and let the tone hold the room.

inner-stillness.name: Inner Stillness
inner-stillness.tagline: Clean tones, no noise, nothing in the way.
inner-stillness.description: A pure 5 Hz theta beat with a soft 528 Hz solfeggio tone and no noise bed. Minimal and quiet.

lotus-drift.name: Lotus Drift
lotus-drift.tagline: Upper theta for a soft, open focus.
lotus-drift.description: A 7 Hz beat for meditations that stay awake but unhurried.

breath-of-earth.name: Breath of Earth
breath-of-earth.tagline: A low 136.1 Hz carrier under deep theta.
breath-of-earth.description: A 4.5 Hz theta beat on a 136.1 Hz carrier, often used in chanting traditions, with grounding brown noise.

crystal-cave.name: Crystal Cave
crystal-cave.tagline: Bright overtones in a dark, still space.
crystal-cave.description: A 6.3 Hz theta beat with a high 852 Hz solfeggio shimmer. Short enough for a lunchtime sit.

earth-resonance.name: Earth Resonance 7.83
earth-resonance.tagline: A 7.83 Hz beat inspired by the Schumann resonance.
earth-resonance.description: The Earth-ionosphere cavity resonates near 7.83 Hz. This session borrows that number as a beat. A fun reference point, not a scientific claim.

heart-tone-528.name: Heart Tone 528
heart-tone-528.tagline: Theta with the well-known 528 Hz tone.
heart-tone-528.description: A 6 Hz theta beat paired with a 528 Hz solfeggio tone for loving-kindness or gratitude practice.

zen-river.name: Zen River
zen-river.description: A 5.5 Hz theta beat over a river-like pink noise bed for longer sits.

mantra-field.name: Mantra Field
mantra-field.tagline: A low hum to repeat your mantra over.
mantra-field.description: A 4.8 Hz beat on a low carrier. Works well with silent or spoken mantra practice.

morning-sit.name: Morning Sit
morning-sit.tagline: Ten minutes before the day gets loud.
morning-sit.description: A short 7.5 Hz session for a daily meditation habit.

body-scan.name: Body Scan
body-scan.tagline: Move attention slowly from feet to crown.
body-scan.description: A 5 Hz theta beat paced for a full body scan practice.

inner-vision.name: Inner Vision
inner-vision.tagline: Theta and a high solfeggio tone for visualization.
inner-vision.description: A 6.5 Hz beat with an 852 Hz layer for guided imagery and visualization practice.

compassion-gamma.name: Compassion Gamma
compassion-gamma.tagline: A fast gamma beat for open-hearted practice.
compassion-gamma.description: Some studies of long-term meditators have recorded strong gamma activity. This 40 Hz session is a nod to that research, not a shortcut to it.

yoga-nidra-delta.name: Yoga Nidra Delta
yoga-nidra-delta.description: A 3 Hz delta beat for yoga nidra and other lying-down practices. Stay aware, or let yourself drift.

alpha-shore.name: Alpha Shore
alpha-shore.description: A 10 Hz alpha beat over pink noise like distant waves. A balanced, easy place to start.

golden-hour.name: Golden Hour
golden-hour.tagline: Warm light, slow breath, loose shoulders.
golden-hour.description: A 9 Hz alpha beat with warm brown noise for the end of the workday.

tea-break.name: Tea Break
tea-break.description: A quick 10.5 Hz session for a mid-day pause.

forest-light.name: Forest Light
forest-light.tagline: Dappled alpha with a 639 Hz layer.
forest-light.description: An 8.5 Hz alpha beat with a 639 Hz solfeggio tone and leafy pink noise.

calm-current.name: Calm Current
calm-current.description: An 11 Hz alpha beat. Calm enough to unwind, awake enough to read or sketch.

sunday-float.name: Sunday Float
sunday-float.description: A long 9.5 Hz session for lazy afternoons.

soft-focus.name: Soft Focus
soft-focus.description: A 12 Hz beat with no noise bed. Light and transparent.

release-396.name: Release 396
release-396.description: An 8 Hz alpha beat paired with a 396 Hz solfeggio tone.

harmony-639.name: Harmony 639
harmony-639.description: A 10 Hz alpha beat with a 639 Hz solfeggio layer.

evening-wind-down.name: Evening Wind-Down
evening-wind-down.tagline: A bridge between the day and the night.
evening-wind-down.description: An 8.2 Hz beat that sits at the bottom of alpha, ready to hand off to a sleep session.

seaside-drift.name: Seaside Drift
seaside-drift.description: A 10 Hz alpha beat under long, slow pink noise surf.

hammock-theta.name: Hammock Theta
hammock-theta.tagline: Swaying somewhere between awake and asleep.
hammock-theta.description: A 6 Hz theta beat for deep relaxation without the goal of sleep.

deep-work.name: Deep Work
deep-work.tagline: An hour of steady beta for heads-down work.
deep-work.description: A 15 Hz beta beat under brown noise that masks chatter. May support focus during long tasks.

study-flow.name: Study Flow
study-flow.tagline: Low beta for reading and note-taking.
study-flow.description: A 14 Hz beta beat with pink noise, sized for one study block.

laser-beta.name: Laser Beta
laser-beta.description: An 18 Hz beta beat reinforced by an isochronic pulse at the same rate. Keep the volume low.

sprint-25.name: Sprint 25
sprint-25.tagline: One focused sprint. Then take a break.
sprint-25.description: A 25-minute 16 Hz session built around the popular timed-sprint method.

code-zone.name: Code Zone
code-zone.description: A 20 Hz beta beat under brown noise for long, uninterrupted problem solving.

reading-room.name: Reading Room
reading-room.tagline: Quiet, low beta for long reads.
reading-room.description: A 13.5 Hz beat with library-soft pink noise.

creative-flow.name: Creative Flow
creative-flow.description: An 11 Hz alpha beat for brainstorming, writing drafts or sketching.

exam-prep.name: Exam Prep
exam-prep.description: A 16 Hz beta beat for revision sessions.

clarity-741.name: Clarity 741
clarity-741.description: A 14 Hz beta beat paired with a 741 Hz solfeggio layer.

steady-mind.name: Steady Mind
steady-mind.tagline: Two hours at the bottom of beta.
steady-mind.description: A 13 Hz beat for long, calm concentration.

writers-room.name: Writer's Room
writers-room.description: A 15 Hz beta beat for writing sessions.

gamma-insight.name: Gamma Insight
gamma-insight.description: A 35 Hz gamma beat with an isochronic pulse. Short by design. Keep the volume low.

attention-40.name: Attention 40
attention-40.description: A 40 Hz gamma beat with pink noise. 40 Hz sensory stimulation is an active research area; results so far are early.

morning-rise.name: Morning Rise
morning-rise.tagline: A bright start without the jitters.
morning-rise.description: A 20 Hz beta beat with an isochronic pulse to start the day.

gamma-40.name: Gamma 40
gamma-40.description: A 40 Hz gamma beat with an isochronic layer. Keep the volume low.

bright-spark.name: Bright Spark
bright-spark.description: A 25 Hz beat for a quick lift.

kinetic.name: Kinetic
kinetic.description: A 28 Hz beat with an isochronic pulse for stretching or a walk.

sun-salute.name: Sun Salute
sun-salute.description: An 18 Hz beta beat with a 417 Hz solfeggio layer for morning movement.

peak-gamma.name: Peak Gamma
peak-gamma.description: A 38 Hz gamma beat. Short sessions are best here.

afternoon-lift.name: Afternoon Lift
afternoon-lift.description: A 22 Hz beta beat under brown noise.

workout-pulse.name: Workout Pulse
workout-pulse.description: A 30 Hz beat with an isochronic layer. Use quietly under your own music if you like.

high-gamma.name: High Gamma
high-gamma.tagline: The fastest beat in the catalog.
high-gamma.description: A 44 Hz gamma beat. Fifteen minutes, low volume.

wake-gently.name: Wake Gently
wake-gently.description: A 12 Hz beat that eases you awake before anything faster.

rainforest-theta.name: Rainforest Theta
rainforest-theta.tagline: Canopy birds and soft rain over a 6 Hz theta beat.
rainforest-theta.description: A rainforest soundscape, with distant birds, insects and light rain, layered over a gentle 6 Hz theta beat for meditation.

waterfall-focus.name: Waterfall Focus
waterfall-focus.tagline: A steady waterfall roar that masks distractions.
waterfall-focus.description: The broad, even sound of a waterfall over a 14 Hz beta beat. The roar covers background chatter while you work.

rain-on-leaves.name: Rain on Leaves
rain-on-leaves.tagline: Rainfall on leaves over a slow delta beat.
rain-on-leaves.description: An hour of steady rain with soft droplets, over a 2 Hz delta beat for winding down to sleep.

mountain-stream.name: Mountain Stream
mountain-stream.tagline: A babbling brook and a classic 10 Hz alpha beat.
mountain-stream.description: A shallow stream running over stones, paired with a 10 Hz alpha beat for easy relaxation.

rainforest-nature-only.name: Rainforest Canopy (Nature Only)
rainforest-nature-only.tagline: Just the rainforest. No tones, no headphones needed.
rainforest-nature-only.description: The rainforest soundscape on its own, with no binaural beat. Play it through speakers or headphones.

waterfall-nature-only.name: Waterfall (Nature Only)
waterfall-nature-only.tagline: Just the waterfall. No tones, no headphones needed.
waterfall-nature-only.description: The waterfall soundscape on its own, with no binaural beat. A simple, steady sound for sleep or focus.

deep-sync-surf.name: Deep Sync: Surf Threshold
deep-sync-surf.tagline: Ocean surf and layered tones. No voice, no music.
deep-sync-surf.description: A tones-only Deep Sync program in the classic long-form style: slow ocean surf with several binaural beats layered at once. The main beat walks from alpha down to the theta border and holds there, while a low 4 Hz layer and a soft 1.5 Hz layer sit underneath the whole time. Generated live in your browser.

deep-sync-1.name: Deep Sync I: Orientation
deep-sync-1.tagline: Your first descent, from alpha to theta and back.
deep-sync-1.description: An introduction to the Deep Sync format. The beat begins in relaxed alpha, steps down into theta for a long still stretch, then brings you back up gently. Pink noise smooths each change.

deep-sync-2.name: Deep Sync II: Body Asleep, Mind Awake
deep-sync-2.tagline: Let the body rest while attention stays clear.
deep-sync-2.description: A guided-style program that lowers the beat to the theta-delta border and holds it there, inviting deep physical rest while you stay lightly aware.

deep-sync-3.name: Deep Sync III: Wide Awareness
deep-sync-3.tagline: A longer arc that touches delta.
deep-sync-3.description: Builds on the first two programs with a deeper middle section in delta, then a bright gamma moment before returning to alpha.

deep-sync-4.name: Deep Sync IV: Release & Recharge
deep-sync-4.tagline: Let go, then fill back up.
deep-sync-4.description: Descends from alpha into theta to unwind, then climbs into low beta so you finish refreshed rather than sleepy.

deep-sync-5.name: Deep Sync V: Night Descent
deep-sync-5.tagline: A one-way trip down into delta.
deep-sync-5.description: Starts in alpha and walks the beat down through theta into slow delta. There is no return stage, so you can drift off as it fades.

deep-sync-6.name: Deep Sync VI: Morning Ascent
deep-sync-6.tagline: From drowsy theta to bright beta.
deep-sync-6.description: The reverse of Night Descent. The beat climbs from theta through alpha into beta, matching the way you naturally wake up.

deep-sync-7.name: Deep Sync VII: Free Flow
deep-sync-7.tagline: An hour that breathes between theta and alpha.
deep-sync-7.description: A long, unstructured program that slowly oscillates between theta and alpha, for open-ended meditation or creative reverie.

deep-sync-8.name: Deep Sync VIII: Focus Ladder
deep-sync-8.tagline: Step up into beta, hold, then step down.
deep-sync-8.description: A work-session program. The beat climbs from alpha into mid beta, holds there for the core of the session, and eases back down at the end.

articles.title: How Binaural Beats Work
articles.dek: Two slightly different tones, one in each ear, and a third rhythm your brain creates on its own.
body: Play a 200 Hz tone in your left ear and a 210 Hz tone in your right, and you will hear something that is not in either signal: a soft pulsing at 10 times per second. That pulse is a binaural beat. It is created inside your auditory system, where signals from both ears meet in the brainstem.
## Why headphones matter

The effect depends on each ear hearing only its own tone. Through speakers, both tones reach both ears and mix in the air, which produces an ordinary acoustic beat instead. That is why every Deep Sync program and frequency session here asks for headphones.
## Carrier and beat

Every session has two numbers. The carrier is the tone in your left ear, usually between 100 and 400 Hz, where binaural beats are easiest to hear. The beat is the difference between the ears. In this app the right ear always plays carrier plus beat, so a 200 Hz carrier with a 6 Hz beat sends 200 Hz left and 206 Hz right.
## What happens next

The idea behind brainwave entrainment is that a steady rhythm might nudge brain activity toward the same frequency. That is the claim researchers are still testing. Some studies report small effects on mood, relaxation or attention; others find little or nothing. See What the Research Says for an honest summary.
## Other layers

Many sessions add pink or brown noise to soften the tones and mask background sound. Some add isochronic tones (a single tone switched on and off at the beat rate, which works without headphones) or a solfeggio tone. You can mix all of these in the player.

articles.title: The Brainwave Bands
articles.dek: Delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma: what the names mean and how the catalog uses them.
body: When electrodes on the scalp record brain activity (an EEG), the signal contains rhythms at many speeds at once. Researchers group those rhythms into bands. The boundaries vary a little between textbooks; these are the ones we use to organize sessions.
## Delta, 0.5 to 4 Hz
The slowest rhythms, most prominent in deep, dreamless sleep. Our delta sessions are built for winding down and sleep.
## Theta, 4 to 8 Hz
Common in drowsiness, light sleep and some meditative states. Theta sessions in the catalog are aimed at meditation and the drifting moments before sleep.
## Alpha, 8 to 13 Hz
Often strongest when you are awake and relaxed with your eyes closed. Alpha sessions are designed for calm, easy relaxation.
## Beta, 13 to 30 Hz
Associated with active thinking, problem solving and alert attention. Beta sessions are aimed at focus and work.
## Gamma, 30 Hz and above

The fastest band, linked in research to attention and to how the brain binds information together. 40 Hz in particular is an active research topic. Gamma sessions here are short and should be played quietly.
## A caution about labels
A brain never runs in one band at a time, and listening to a 10 Hz beat does not switch your brain into alpha. The bands are a useful map for choosing a session, not a promise of a particular state.

articles.title: A Short History of the Gateway Experience
articles.dek: How a radio executive's sound experiments ended up in a declassified Army report, and then all over the internet.
body: The story of binaural beats starts in 1839, when the Prussian physicist Heinrich Wilhelm Dove described hearing a beat that existed in neither ear alone. For more than a century it remained a laboratory curiosity.
## Robert Monroe

In the 1950s and 1960s Robert Monroe, a New York radio broadcasting executive, began experimenting with sound as a way to study sleep and altered states. His interest grew after experiences he later described as out-of-body, which he wrote about in his 1971 book Journeys Out of the Body. He went on to found a research and education center in Virginia, known today as The Monroe Institute.

Monroe developed and patented an audio technique that layered tones to produce binaural beats intended to help listeners reach particular states. The Gateway Experience, a home-study program of guided recordings, organized those states into numbered stages, moving the listener step by step from relaxation toward deeper states of awareness.
## The 1983 Army report

In 1983 Lieutenant Colonel Wayne McDonnell of the U.S. Army wrote a report titled Analysis and Assessment of Gateway Process. It tried to explain the Gateway program using the physics and psychology ideas of the day, some of them speculative. The CIA declassified the document in 2003 and later made it available in its online reading room.
## The internet rediscovers it

Around 2020 and 2021 the report went viral on forums and short-video apps, often described as proof that the government had unlocked secret powers. The report itself is better read as one officer's assessment of an unusual training program than as evidence of anything supernatural.
## Where Deep Sync fits

Our Deep Sync programs borrow the general idea of the format, long sessions that layer binaural beats over noise and step through bands over time. They are original compositions generated live in your browser. They are not affiliated with or endorsed by The Monroe Institute, and they use none of its recordings or trademarks.

articles.title: What the Research Says (and Doesn't)
articles.dek: An honest look at the evidence for binaural beats. Short version: it's mixed.
body: Binaural beats are popular, but the science is still unsettled. Here is a plain-language summary of where things stand.
## Some positive findings

A 2019 meta-analysis by Garcia-Argibay and colleagues pooled dozens of studies and found small-to-moderate average effects of binaural beats on memory, attention, anxiety and pain perception. The authors also noted large differences between studies, depending on factors such as beat frequency, exposure time and whether the beats were masked by noise.
## Mixed evidence for entrainment

A 2023 systematic review by Ingendoh and colleagues looked specifically at EEG studies asking whether binaural beats actually pull brain rhythms toward the beat frequency. Results were inconsistent: some studies found the expected changes, others found none, and some found the opposite.
## Why results vary

Many studies are small, use different frequencies and durations, and are hard to blind, because people usually know what they are listening to. Expectation and simple relaxation (lying still with headphones on, away from screens) can produce real benefits on their own.
## How we talk about it

That is why we say sessions may support relaxation, focus, or sleep, and why we never claim they treat or cure anything. If you enjoy a session and it helps you rest or concentrate, that is a fine reason to use it. If you have a health condition, talk to a clinician first; frequency sessions are not a substitute for care.

articles.title: Isochronic Tones, Solfeggio and Noise Colors
articles.dek: The optional layers in the player, explained.
body: Binaural beats are the core of every session, but the player can mix in three more layers.
## Isochronic tones

An isochronic tone is a single tone that switches on and off at a steady rate. Unlike a binaural beat, the rhythm is in the sound itself, so it works through speakers. It is also more noticeable, so keep it low.
## Solfeggio tones

The solfeggio frequencies (174, 285, 396, 417, 528, 639, 741, 852 and 963 Hz) became popular in the 1970s and later through New Age books. Claims about their specific healing properties are not supported by scientific evidence. Many listeners simply enjoy them as pleasant, steady tones, which is how we offer them.
## Pink and brown noise

White noise has equal energy at every frequency and sounds hissy. Pink noise rolls off the highs and sounds more like steady rain. Brown noise rolls off even more and sounds like a deep rumble or distant surf. Both are useful for masking background sounds, and some small studies suggest pink noise may support deeper sleep, though evidence is limited.

articles.title: Listening Safely
articles.dek: Five simple rules for using frequency sessions.
body: ## Use headphones
Binaural beats only work when each ear hears its own tone. Use the left/right channel test in the player to check your headphones are on the right way round.
## Keep the volume low
The tones should sit just above the threshold of hearing, like a quiet room tone. Louder is not better, and long sessions at high volume can harm your hearing.
## Never while driving
Some sessions are designed to make you drowsy. Do not listen while driving, cycling, or operating machinery.
## Epilepsy and seizure disorders
If you have epilepsy or a seizure disorder, check with a doctor before listening to rhythmic audio. The visualizer is deliberately gentle, and you can switch it off.
## Stop if it doesn't feel right
If you feel discomfort, headache, anxiety or dizziness, stop the session. These sessions may support relaxation, focus, or sleep, but they are not medical treatment.
